problem: Imitation learning and IRL for socially compliant robot navigation lack large-scale, real-world demonstration datasets. Prior datasets are simulated (e.g., social-force 'experts'), small (THÖR ~1 h, JRDB 64 min), indoor-only or orchestrated, perception-focused, or recorded with robots that are not driven in a socially aware way. None of them provide socially compliant motion commands.
motivation: Social navigation is hard to specify as a reward because it is multi-objective, but humans can easily demonstrate it. Learning from Demonstration therefore needs natural, in-the-wild human-teleoperated robot trajectories with the joystick commands attached. The authors also argue that there is more than one socially compliant strategy for a given scene, and that robots with different morphologies (legged vs wheeled) may navigate socially in different ways.
key_idea: Release SCAND, a large multi-modal dataset of human-teleoperated, socially compliant robot navigation on a university campus: 8.7 h, 138 trajectories, 25 miles, on a legged Spot and a wheeled Jackal, with joystick commands and social-interaction tags. Show that behavior cloning on it yields socially compliant global and local planners.
insight: A demonstrator classifier reaches 74.48% accuracy (vs 50% chance) at telling apart two demonstrators driving the same route from 10-second windows, which suggests socially compliant navigation is multi-modal across people. A simple behavior-cloning agent trained on SCAND, without any representation pretraining, cuts the Hausdorff distance to the demonstrated path from 1.25 (move_base) to 0.26. In a 14-participant real-robot study it is rated significantly more socially compliant and safer than move_base, so even naive imitation on in-the-wild demonstrations captures social behavior that a geometric planner misses.
method: Data collection: 4 human demonstrators teleoperate Spot and Jackal with a joystick while walking about 2 m behind the robot. Recording is on UT Austin campus sidewalks, roads, lawns and indoors, at peak foot traffic, including football game days, with no orchestrated scenarios.

Sensors and logging: both robots carry a VLP-16 lidar (10 Hz), a 6D IMU (16 Hz) and a front Azure Kinect RGB (20 Hz). The Jackal adds a stereo camera and wheel odometry; the Spot adds 5 monocular cameras, visual odometry and leg joint angles. Joystick (v, ω) commands and frame transforms are included, all recorded as rosbags via the AMRL stack.

Social interaction tags: every trajectory is annotated with a list of 12 predefined labels, e.g. against/with traffic, street crossing, overtaking, passing conversational groups, blind corner, narrow doorway, crossing stationary queue, stairs, vehicle interaction, large crowds.

Demonstrator classifier: takes 10 s windows of BEV grayscale lidar (1 Hz, 4-layer CNN), relative poses, the 200-point future trajectory, IMU and joystick (3-layer MLP). A 3-layer MLP head trained with BCE predicts which of two demonstrators drove. It is trained on 12 and validated on 4 trajectories from the same route.

Behavior-cloning global and local planner: shared encoder over 2 s of BEV lidar (2 Hz), relative poses and IMU, plus move_base's global plan and desired velocities toward the pose 10 m ahead as a prior. Two 3-layer MLP heads predict the 200-point demonstrated path (10 m horizon) and 20 timesteps of joystick (v, ω). The two MSE losses are summed and trained jointly end-to-end.

setting.backbone: 4-layer CNN (BEV lidar) + MLP encoders with MLP heads, behavior cloning (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: SCAND Spot trajectories, 75% train split (full SCAND: 138 trajectories, 8.7 h, 25 miles on Spot + Jackal); classifier uses 16 trajectories from 2 demonstrators on one route
setting.observation: BEV grayscale 3D-lidar images + relative odometry poses + IMU + move_base global plan / desired velocities
setting.action_space: continuous velocity (v, ω) for 20 future timesteps (local planner) + 200-point path over 10 m horizon (global planner)
setting.privileged: In offline evaluation, the move_base prior is computed toward the demonstrator's actual position 10 m in the future (goal taken from the demonstration). Otherwise none.

numbers.eval_set_note: held-out test set of Spot trajectories (paper provides 75%-25% train-test split of Spot trajectories)
numbers.extra: uses move_base global plan / desired velocities as input prior; lower Hausdorff is better
numbers.evidence: Sec. IV-B2: 'after training the BC global planner agent on SCAND, the average Hausdorff distance between the predicted trajectory and the demonstrated trajectory is improved at 0.26'

numbers.eval_set_note: 16 Spot trajectories by two demonstrators on the same route (Speedway road); trained on 12, evaluated on 4 held-out; 10-second windows
numbers.evidence: Sec. IV-A2: 'the classifier is 74.48% accurate at classifying the expert on the held-out test set'

numbers.eval_set_note: real-world Spot trials indoors with 14 human participants, static and dynamic scenarios; 1-5 Likert ratings
numbers.extra: subjective questionnaire scores (mean), compared against move_base
numbers.evidence: Sec. IV-B2 / Fig. 7: 'SCAND mean=4.39, sd=0.99; move_base mean=2.86 ... safer (SCAND mean=4.71, sd=0.70; move_base mean=2.89'

numbers_note: Dataset paper with no standard navigation benchmark. Results are offline Hausdorff distance, classifier accuracy, and a small human-rating study (also shown in Fig. 7). There are no SR/SPL-style metrics and no Jackal-based experiments.
results: SCAND provides 138 trajectories (8.7 h, 25 miles, about 40 km) of socially compliant teleoperation on two robots with 12 interaction tags. It is larger and more naturalistic than JRDB (64 min) and THÖR (1 h, indoor, orchestrated). BC trained on SCAND reduces the Hausdorff distance to the demonstrated path from 1.25 (move_base) to 0.26. In real-world trials with 14 participants, the BC local planner was rated more socially compliant (4.39 vs 2.86) and safer (4.71 vs 2.89) than move_base, both at p<0.001 (ANOVA).
limitations: Collected only on one campus in Austin, TX, so it may encode regional norms such as keeping right and overtaking on the left. Rare interactions are under-represented.
Validation is preliminary: simple BC, only a move_base baseline, Spot data only, two simple indoor human-study scenarios, and no standardized benchmark or success metrics.
No human detection or tracking annotations; tags are per-trajectory text labels only, not time-localized.
